Sataniv Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Sataniv's Jewish community, present from 1532, survived Tatar raids in the 1530s, the Khmelnytsky massacres of 1651, and a Haidamak rebellion in 1703. Rabbi Leib Segal-Geller represented Podolia in the Council of Four Lands, the supreme Jewish self-governing body documented at Kremenets and Kulykiv elsewhere in this collection. In 1756, Rabbi Mendel of Sataniv sat on a rabbinical court that held a formal public trial of followers of Jacob Frank's movement, another thread documented at several towns throughout this collection. In the late 18th century, the local Hasidic community was headed by Israel Geleenter, known as the Magid of Sataniv, an adherent of the Baal Shem Tov himself; later, Rabbi Hanoch-Genoch (1800–1884) founded his own Hasidic court, and both Husiatin and Zinkov Hasidim, documented elsewhere in this collection, maintained synagogues in the town. In 1913, a newly opened cinema screened a film dedicated to the life of Jewish colonists in Eretz Israel. During a 1919 pogrom staged by the Ukrainian People's Republic army, three soldiers of the town's own Jewish self-defense detachment were killed; earlier that year, four Jewish soldiers drafted into the same army had been murdered by their own fellow soldiers. On May 14–15, 1942, 240 Jews were walled up alive in the cellars of an old house; 647 were executed in total during the occupation.
